name: LITTLE SWISS BUNSHINE BURGER - (Comes on a buttered bun)

recipe.history:
Swiss cheese — properly called Emmental or Emmentaler — was born in the green, fog-draped valleys of the Bernese Oberland in central Switzerland, most famously along the Emme River valley from which it takes its name. Records of its production date as far back as 1293, when alpine dairying communities in the Swiss Alps developed the cheese as a practical way to preserve the surplus milk produced during the lush summer grazing season. Herdsmen would drive cattle up to high-altitude pastures, called alps, each spring, and the rich, fatty milk collected there was transformed into large, dense wheels of cheese that could survive the long trek back down to the valleys. The characteristic holes — known formally as "eyes" and colloquially as the thing that makes Swiss cheese unmistakably Swiss — are the result of carbon dioxide gas released by Propionibacterium freudenreichii bacteria during the aging process. Wheels were traditionally massive, often weighing over 200 pounds, and a single wheel required over 250 liters of milk to produce. For centuries, Emmental remained a regional treasure, traded at markets in Bern and Lucerne, prized for its mild, nutty sweetness and the way it melted into a silken, cohesive sheet rather than breaking apart.

Swiss cheese crossed the Atlantic in the early nineteenth century as part of a broader wave of European dairy culture, but it was the mid-twentieth century American cheeseburger boom that truly cemented its place on the American grill. As burger joints proliferated across the country after World War II, cooks discovered that Swiss cheese behaved differently from American singles or cheddar — it melted more slowly, stayed cohesive, and contributed a subtler, less aggressive flavor that let the beef shine rather than compete with it. Diner cooks working flat-top griddles found they could lay a slice of Swiss over a patty, tent it with a small dome or a splash of water, and coax it into a perfectly draped, molten sheet in under a minute. The mild nuttiness of Emmental complemented the Maillard-browned crust of a smash patty without overwhelming the palate. By the 1970s, the "Swiss burger" had become a diner staple from coast to coast, a menu fixture that signaled a certain refinement — a step up from the plain cheeseburger without requiring the theatrics of blue cheese or the sharpness of aged cheddar. Today, Swiss remains one of the most requested burger cheeses in America, a bridge between old-world alpine craftsmanship and the purely American art of the hamburger.

I still remember the first time I understood what Swiss cheese could do on a burger. I was maybe nine years old, sitting at a low Formica counter at a diner outside of Albany, New York — the kind of place with a pie case lit up like a reliquary and a cook who never once looked up from the griddle. My father ordered for both of us, and when my plate arrived there was a burger on it with a thick, translucent-edged slice of Swiss draped over the patty like a warm blanket, the edges slightly lacey and crisped against the cast iron. I didn't know the word Emmental. I didn't know about the Bernese Oberland or Propionibacterium. I just knew that when I bit into it, the cheese stretched and pulled in a way that felt generous, almost slow, and that the gentle nuttiness of it made the beef taste more like itself rather than less. It was a revelation dressed up as an ordinary Tuesday lunch. I've been chasing that moment at every griddle I've stood in front of since.

Cooking a burger to medium rare is not a preference — it is a philosophy, a commitment to the idea that meat has a point of maximum expression and that the cook's job is to find it and stop there. The window is 130–135°F, fifty-four to fifty-seven degrees Celsius, and inside that window the proteins have tightened just enough to give the patty structure and a proper crust while the center remains pink, warm, and yielding, the fat rendered but not driven out, the juices still held in suspension rather than pooled on the plate. Beyond 135°F you are no longer cooking — you are evicting. Every degree past that threshold is moisture and flavor leaving the building, the fat seizing, the texture tightening toward something that requires condiments to rescue it. A medium rare burger needs no rescue. It arrives complete: crust, warmth, juice, fat in balance. The buttered brioche bun exists to receive it, not to compensate for it. This is the contract between cook and diner, and the thermometer is how you honor it.
ingredients: 8 oz (225g) ground beef, 80/20 lean-to-fat ratio, freshly ground chuck preferred
2 slices Emmental (Swiss) cheese, cut approximately 1/4 inch thick
1 tablespoon unsalted butter, softened, for buttering the bun
1 teaspoon neutral oil (such as canola or grapeseed), for the cooking surface
1 leaf green leaf or butter lettuce
2 slices ripe tomato, cut 1/4 inch thick
2–3 thin slices white or yellow onion
1 teaspoon yellow or Dijon mustard (optional, for bun)
instructions: 1. Remove the ground beef from the refrigerator 20–30 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Divide into two equal 4 oz portions and gently form each into a round patty roughly 4 inches in diameter and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty with your thumb — this prevents the patty from doming as it cooks. Season generously on both sides with kosher salt and freshly cracked black pepper immediately before cooking.

2. Set a cast iron skillet or heavy stainless griddle over medium-high heat and allow it to preheat for at least 3 minutes until the surface is very hot. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat, letting it come to a shimmer.

3. Place the seasoned patties in the skillet. Do not press them down. Cook undisturbed for 3–4 minutes until a deep brown crust has formed on the underside — check by lifting one edge gently with a spatula. Flip the patties once.

4. Immediately after flipping, lay one slice of Swiss cheese on top of each patty. Add 1–2 tablespoons of water to the edge of the pan (not on the patties) and cover the skillet with a lid or a large heatproof bowl to trap steam. This will melt the cheese rapidly and evenly without overcooking the meat.

5. Continue cooking for 2–3 minutes, checking the internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer inserted into the side of the patty at the center. Remove the patties from the heat when they register 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. The cheese should be fully melted, glossy, and draped over the sides of the patty.
6. Transfer the patties to a wire rack or clean plate and allow them to rest for 3–5 minutes. Do not skip the rest — the internal temperature will rise 3–5 degrees and the juices will redistribute.

7. While the patties rest, wipe the skillet and return it to medium heat. Spread the softened unsalted butter generously over the cut faces of the brioche bun halves. Place them butter-side down in the skillet and toast until golden brown and slightly crisp, 1–2 minutes. Watch carefully — brioche burns quickly due to its sugar content.

8. Assemble the burger: spread mayonnaise and/or mustard on the toasted bun faces if using. Place the lettuce leaf on the bottom bun, followed by the tomato slices and onion. Set the rested, Swiss-topped patties on top. Add the pickle slices. Cap with the top bun.
9. Serve immediately. The patty must be served at medium rare — 130–135°F (54–57°C) internal temperature. No exceptions.
